title: Interview Candidates for Your Startup
summary: Learn effective strategies for interviewing candidates for your startup, including tips from evaluating skills and cultural fit to making hiring decisions.
body_markdown:
Knowing how to[interview candidates for your startup](https://www.dover.com/) comes down to planning each round before the first call happens. Early teams have little room for a bad hire, so every stage has to show whether someone can do the job, work well with your team, and still be interested by the time an offer arrives. This guide covers how to prepare, which question types to use, how to structure the process from screening call to offer, and what to watch for when interviews happen remotely.


**TLDR:**


-


Structure your startup interview process across 5 stages: screening call, hiring manager interview, technical assessment, onsite, and offer.


-


Use all three question types (technical, behavioral, situational) to assess both skills and cultural fit together.


-


Schedule the next interview round within 24 hours of each stage to avoid losing top candidates to competing offers.


-


Remote interviews now carry deepfake fraud risk; confirm identity across rounds and get consent before using AI notetakers.


-


Some free ATS tools include unlimited users, jobs, and candidates with customizable interview plans at no cost.


## Preparing for the Interview


Top candidates prepare for the interview, so you should too. Your hiring team should sync to clearly define what you want out of a candidate, come up with thoughtful interview questions, make sure all interviewers are ready to communicate your company’s vision, determine what qualities the ideal candidate should have, and review each resume beforehand so questions fit the candidate’s experience.


## Interview Questions Breakdown


[Asking the right interview questions](https://www.dover.com/hiring-guides/how-to-choose-interview-questions) isn’t some hidden alchemical secret, but it does help to make sure you’re covering all of your bases. Have a list of technical, behavioral and situational questions ready to ask candidates that assess their knowledge, skills and ability to think critically. Let’s take a closer look at each category:


-


**Technical questions:** These determine if a candidate has the skills and knowledge necessary for the role. For instance, you might ask a software engineer about their experience with programming languages your team uses.


-


**Behavioral questions:** These give you a sense of who a candidate is and how they work. These questions aren’t technical, and give candidates a chance to talk about themselves and how they’ve handled work in the past. These questions usually begin with, “Tell me a time when…,” or, “Give me an example of …”


-


**Situational questions:** These give your candidates hypothetical scenarios to gauge how they use critical thinking and problem-solving. For example, you might ask, “How would you handle a disagreement between you and a team member over a project’s direction?”


Your questions should be tailored to each role and its requirements, but they should also help you assess if they’d be a good cultural fit for your startup. It can also be helpful to ask follow-up questions and leave some time at the end for more free-flowing conversation. Having a more natural conversation with the candidate, if time allows, gives you a chance to get to know them better.


## How to Structure the Interview Process


A structured interview process is a simple and organized interview process. By having a set structure in place, you can optimize your interview flow and make sure no time is wasted while gathering as much relevant information as you can about the candidate. A clear, simple interview plan also helps candidates go through the pipeline quickly without withdrawing before the offer stage. Generally, you can structure your startup interview process with these steps:


### 1. Screening Call


The[screening call](https://www.dover.com/hiring-guides/how-to-do-phone-screens) is the first step and screens potential candidates to confirm they’re qualified for the role. This is usually a fairly short interview handled by HR or a recruiter. The screening call acts as a filter for candidates who may have gotten through the resume screenings but aren’t a good fit.


### 2. Hiring Manager Interview


The next phase is usually with a hiring manager, and this is a longer, more in-depth interview than the screening call. This is a good chance to get into some behavioral and situational questions, as well as determine if they’re a good cultural fit for the company.


### 3. Technical Interviews / Take Home Assignment


If they’re applying for a technical role within the company, this stage will test them on their skills. It could include take-home assignments and interviewing with technical questions to see if they can handle the responsibilities of their role. For non-technical roles, take home assignments or case studies are given to assess how candidates would handle workplace scenarios.


### 4. Onsite


The onsite is typically the longest stage in the interview process and often involves multiple interviews with leadership and other stakeholders from different teams. The onsite may also be conducted over several days or there is a final interview with the CEO or a founder.


### 5. Offer


The final stage is making an offer. Once you’ve found the right hire, make an offer quickly that’s commensurate with their experience and benchmarks for the position.


To keep candidates engaged and in the interview pipeline, you should make sure to schedule the next interviews within 24 hours of each round. This way you don’t lose out on top candidates by making them wait too long.


**Startup interview stages at a glance**


Stage Format What it covers


Screening call Short call handled by HR or a recruiter Confirms the candidate is qualified for the role


Hiring manager interview Longer, in-depth conversation Behavioral and situational questions, plus cultural fit


Technical interview or take-home assignment Technical questions, take-home work, or case studies for non-technical roles Skills and how a candidate would handle the responsibilities of the role


Onsite Multiple interviews with leadership and stakeholders, sometimes over several days Fit across teams, often ending with a final interview with the CEO or a founder


Offer Prompt offer with salary, benefits, and other details Compensation benchmarked to experience and the position, with room to negotiate


## Assessing Candidate’s Skills and Experience


Assessing a candidate’s skills and experience is one of the more obvious steps of the interview process, but this is where some startups get stuck. You want candidates with the right skills for the role, but avoid hiring someone who can only do one thing really well. At startups, candidates with diverse and versatile skill sets are especially useful because they often wear a lot of hats and jump between projects as the needs of the business shift.


With that being said, technical roles can be tested through practical assessments such as coding challenges, take-home assessments and other tests that gauge their abilities. For non-technical roles, you can focus on asking questions about past experience and accomplishments. This is where those behavioral and situational questions we talked about earlier come in handy.


## Assessing Cultural Fit for Startups


Cultural fit should never be undervalued during the interview process. At startups, your team defines your culture and workplace. You should always focus on finding people who align with your company’s goals and vision, as this leads to more long-term hires who want to grow with the company. To assess cultural fit, ask questions about a candidate’s work preferences, values and how they handle conflict.


## Making a Decision


The penultimate step in the interview process is making a decision. You should meet with all interviewers and stakeholders to compare notes and talk about the candidates in the running. Come to a consensus on who is the best fit for the company from both a skill perspective and a cultural perspective. At Dover, we recommend all interviewers complete a feedback form that scores candidates. At the end of the interview process, we recommend that the hiring team and interviewers[debrief about each candidate](https://www.dover.com/hiring-guides/interview-debriefs) - their strengths and weakness - and recommend if they should be hired. Once you’ve decided on who is the best fit for your company, you can extend an offer.


## Extending an Offer


Finally,[extend an offer](https://www.dover.com/hiring-guides/how-to-make-an-offer) to your top candidate. Make the offer promptly so you don’t lose them to another opportunity. Include salary, benefits and other key details so they have what they need to decide. Set a reasonable response window, one that encourages a quick answer but still leaves room for questions. Be prepared to negotiate, especially with an experienced candidate who checks all of your boxes.


## Interviewing in Late 2026: Identity Checks and AI Notice Rules


Two developments change how startups run interviews this year. The first is candidate identity. SHRM has reported on[how employers are confronting deepfake interview fraud](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/how-employers-are-confronting-deepfake-interview-fraud) , and remote-first startups are a target since most interviews happen on video. A few habits help: confirm the person on camera matches the application, ask unscripted follow-up questions, and have a later-round interviewer meet the candidate again. For roles with access to code, customer data, or company systems, add a live identity check before the offer.


The second is notice and consent when AI touches the process. Illinois’s[HB 3773](https://legiscan.com/IL/bill/HB3773/2023) took effect on January 1, 2026, and requires employers to tell workers when they use AI in hiring decisions, and its AI Video Interview Act calls for notice and consent before AI analyzes recorded interviews. Colorado’s[replacement AI law](https://legiscan.com/CO/bill/SB189/2026) is slated to start on January 1, 2027. If you use an AI notetaker such as the one in Dover’s Premium plan, tell candidates and get consent where required, and check with employment counsel before you finalize your process.


## Common Recruiting Mistakes to Avoid


No company is immune to recruiting mistakes. But, there are some common mistakes that many startups make that you can plan to avoid. These common mistakes include:


-


**Not casting a wide net:** Maybe you’ve made one or two great hires off LinkedIn, but that doesn’t mean you should be limiting your job listings to only one job board. Casting too small of a net could cause you to miss out on a lot of candidates. Take advantage of multiple channels like job boards, employee referrals and other sourcing options to widen your net.


-


**Rushing:** Make sure you don’t rush the interview process just because you need to fill a role fast. Taking shortcuts could lead to bad decisions and costly turnover. Take the time to thoroughly vet candidates and make the right choice the first time.


-


**Lagging:** On the flip side, taking too long can also be detrimental. A slow, inefficient hiring process wastes time and could cause you to lose out on top talent. Make sure your hiring process is thorough but efficient.


-


**Hyper-fixing on technical skills:** Technical skills are important, but requiring super-specific expertise can hamstring your hiring efforts. Adaptable generalists are sometimes the best hires you can make.


-


**Undervaluing cultural fit:** Cultural fit should always be a major priority for startups. You want to maintain a healthy culture that pushes your mission forward and makes the work environment enjoyable for everyone.


-


**Avoid hiring tools and resources:** Some startups can get too tight with their budgets and avoid hiring software and other resources that can actually save them money in the long run. ## FAQs


### What should a free applicant tracking system include for a team just starting to hire?


A free ATS fits a first-time hiring team when it has no cap on users, jobs, or candidates, because a cap can force a migration right when hiring picks up. Look for customizable interview plans, scheduling links, and job board posting in the free tier. Paid ATS options often price per company on annual contracts, which tends to suit teams with a dedicated recruiting ops owner, while founder-led hiring usually needs something that works on day one without an implementation project. Features like AI notetaking and multi-calendar scheduling are typically reserved for paid tiers, so it helps to check what sits behind the paywall before committing.


### What hiring tools do YC-backed startups use?


There is no single standard stack, and the mix usually changes with stage and hiring volume. Early teams commonly pair an ATS (options include Ashby, Greenhouse, Lever, Workable, or a free plan such as Dover’s) with a sourcing channel like LinkedIn and a startup-focused job board such as Y Combinator’s Work at a Startup. As hiring volume grows, many add outside recruiting support, including fractional recruiters who work inside the same ATS. Y Combinator startups are among the teams that have used Dover, though the right mix depends on how many roles you hire each year and who owns recruiting.


### How many interview rounds should a startup have?


Most startups land somewhere between three and five rounds, with fewer for junior or non-technical roles and more for senior or technical ones. Each round should test something the previous one did not, such as basic qualifications, role depth, hands-on skills, and team fit, so candidates are not asked the same questions twice. Adding rounds beyond that often slows the process and raises the chance a strong candidate accepts another offer first.
